title: Seizure Management
summary: Responding safely and effectively to a patient experiencing a generalized seizure.
equipment: Oxygen delivery device (NRB or nasal cannula)
Seizure medications available (lorazepam, diazepam, levetiracetam per order)
steps: If seizure occurs: stay with the patient and note the exact time seizure began.
Call for help — activate emergency response if this is a first seizure or seizure >5 minutes.
Protect from injury: lower patient to bed/floor if standing. Remove sharp objects from surroundings. Lower side rails and pad if applicable.
Turn patient to lateral (recovery) position — reduces aspiration risk.
Do NOT restrain extremities during active seizure — you will cause injury. Do NOT put anything in the mouth.
Maintain airway: position jaw, clear secretions if needed with suction after convulsive phase ends.
Apply oxygen per protocol (2–4 L/min nasal cannula or NRB if needed) after the convulsive phase.
Monitor and document: seizure type (focal vs. generalized), body parts affected, eye deviation, duration, level of consciousness.
If IV access: administer anticonvulsant medications per order (lorazepam 2–4 mg IV is first-line for active seizure).
If no IV: rectal diazepam or buccal/nasal midazolam per protocol.
Status epilepticus (seizure >5 min or 2+ seizures without recovery): emergency. Escalate immediately.
Post-ictal phase: assess LOC, neurological status, airway, SpO2, vital signs. Reorient patient.
Document: onset time, duration, seizure characteristics, interventions, post-ictal status.
nursing_considerations: NEVER put anything in a seizing patient's mouth — this is a myth, causes injury to patient and nurse.
Status epilepticus (>5 minutes) is a neurological emergency — call code/STAT if not already done.
Document seizure characteristics comprehensively — helps classify seizure type and adjust medications.
After a breakthrough seizure: assess for triggers (missed medications, electrolyte imbalance, infection, fever, toxicity).
Post-ictal confusion can last minutes to hours — protect the patient from falls during this period.

title: Fall Prevention Protocol
summary: Implementing a comprehensive inpatient fall prevention program for high-risk patients.
equipment: Fall risk wristband and door signage
steps: Complete and document fall risk assessment on admission and per policy (see Fall Risk Assessment procedure for Morse Scale scoring).
Implement universal fall precautions for ALL patients regardless of risk score:
Bed in lowest locked position. Call light within reach. Non-slip footwear on.
Personal items, water, and phone within reach. Hourly rounding.
For moderate/high risk patients (Morse ≥25), add:
Bed exit alarm — confirm it is ON and functional each shift.
Fall risk identification (colored wristband per facility policy, door signage).
Assistive device at bedside and confirmed that patient knows to use it.
Ensure patient can verbalize when and how to call for help.
Toilet patient before leaving the room and at the start of each shift.
Consider bedside commode to reduce transfer distance.
Medication review: identify and flag high-risk medications (sedatives, opioids, diuretics, antihypertensives, hypoglycemics).
For very high risk or confused patients: consider a safety companion/sitter, low bed with floor mat, frequent monitoring.
Patient and family education: explain fall risks, when to call for help, safe ambulation, footwear.
Post-fall: complete incident report, full assessment (vital signs, neuro check, injury assessment), notify provider, family, and charge nurse. Implement post-fall huddle.
Document all fall prevention interventions in the care plan.
nursing_considerations: Falls with injury are never events in many hospital programs — thorough documentation of preventive measures is critical.
Bed alarms create alarm fatigue if not calibrated properly — confirm sensitivity and placement each shift.
Patients often underreport dizziness or weakness — proactively assess with standing transfer and observe gait.
Post-fall huddle (5–15 min debrief with the care team) identifies system failures and prevents repeat falls.
Never leave a high-risk patient alone in the bathroom — wait outside the door or stay with them.

title: Patient Positioning & Log Rolling
summary: Safely repositioning patients to prevent pressure injuries, maintain spinal alignment, or post-procedure recovery.
equipment: Additional nurses as needed (2+ for log roll)
steps: Assess patient: mobility, pain, weight, spinal precautions, post-op restrictions, skin breakdown risk.
Reposition at minimum every 2 hours for immobile patients — use a turning schedule.
Supine positioning: HOB ≤30° (unless contraindicated). Pillow under head (not above shoulders). Heels elevated off mattress. Arms at sides with palms down. Maintain spinal alignment.
Semi-Fowler's: HOB 30–45°. Used for respiratory support, tube feedings, and after meals.
Fowler's: HOB 60–90°. Supports breathing, oral intake.
Lateral/Side-lying: 30° lateral tilt (avoid 90°). Place pillow between knees, under top arm, and at back. Off-load trochanter.
Prone positioning (ARDS protocol): requires 4–6 nurses, advanced team. Used for severe ARDS to improve oxygenation. Requires specialized turning and positioning.
Log Roll (spinal precautions):
Position 3 nurses on same side of bed. One at head, one at torso, one at legs.
Nurse at head maintains manual cervical stabilization in-line with body axis throughout.
On count of 3: roll patient as ONE UNIT — head, spine, and legs move simultaneously.
Do not twist or flex spine. Place pillow between knees and maintain straight spinal alignment in lateral position.
Transfers: use gait belt for all ambulation assistance. Standby assist vs. full assist vs. 2-person lift — match to patient assessment.
Document: repositioning time, position used, skin assessment, patient tolerance.
nursing_considerations: Heels are the second most common pressure injury site — off-load completely using heel suspension boots or calf pillows.
Shear forces (sliding down in bed) are as damaging as direct pressure — use repositioning sheets and adjust HOB to minimize shear.
Log roll requires practice and team communication — assign roles before initiating.
Prone positioning carries high complication risk (facial pressure injuries, ETT dislodgement, line complications) — follow a structured protocol.
Use safe patient handling equipment (ceiling lifts, repositioning aids) to protect both patient and nurse.

title: Restraint Application & Monitoring
summary: Applying and monitoring physical restraints as a last resort when less restrictive interventions have failed.
equipment: Soft wrist restraints or mitt restraints (per type ordered)
steps: Verify provider order: type of restraint, clinical indication, and time limit.
Confirm that less restrictive alternatives have been attempted and documented: redirection, reorientation, family presence, activity devices, repositioning.
Explain the restraint rationale to patient/family. Obtain consent per facility policy.
Perform hand hygiene. Apply restraint per manufacturer instructions.
Soft wrist restraints: apply with enough slack that 2 fingers fit under the restraint. Tie with a clove hitch or quick-release knot to bed frame (NOT side rail).
Ensure proper circulation: assess skin color, capillary refill, sensation, and movement distal to restraint.
Position patient comfortably with HOB elevated and call light within reach.
Assess and document every 2 hours (or per facility policy):
Behavior requiring restraint. Neurovascular check (CMS: circulation, movement, sensation).
Skin integrity under and around restraint. Restraint position and security.
Attempt to use least restrictive alternative at each assessment.
Remove restraint at least every 2 hours (per shift) for ROM exercises, toileting, nutrition.
Reassess ongoing need for restraint every shift — document justification for continuing.
Discontinue as soon as clinically safe — restraint use should be minimal and time-limited.
Document all assessments, alternatives attempted, and discontinuation.
nursing_considerations: Restraints are a last resort — they do NOT prevent falls, they can cause injury, and they increase agitation in confused patients.
Respiratory complications: patients in wrist restraints can develop aspiration and asphyxiation — maintain HOB ≥30° and monitor closely.
Never tie restraints to side rails — side rail lowering can cause serious injury from restraint tension.
Regulatory requirement: restrained patients must be assessed every 2 hours — non-compliance is a major survey finding.
Alternatives to try first: bed alarm, medication review (reduce sedating agents), scheduled toileting, family at bedside, diversional activities, soft arm immobilizers.
